It reaches the baselines' final quality with far fewer evaluations and comparable cost. On twelve equation discovery problems, it recovers the ground-truth structure of more equations than No-analysis and existing language-model and genetic programming baselines.

Computer-use agents increasingly handle private information and act on users' behalf across desktop and web applications, including email. Phishing therefore poses privacy and security risks that depend not only on whether agents recognize malicious messages, but also on how they respond. Existing phishing datasets were developed primarily for conventional detection, leaving agent susceptibility to persuasive malicious requests insufficiently characterized. To expose vulnerabilities that pre-existing datasets may miss, we introduce AgentPhishing, a benchmark for evaluating whether persuasive phishing attacks can evade detection and induce LLM email agents to comply with malicious requests. We develop PhishOpt, which optimizes reusable email-generation skills against individual agents under fixed benchmark constraints and a realism constraint. We analyze the generated emails using Cialdini's persuasion principles to identify strategies associated with agent failures and use these findings to construct a universal generation skill. Our evaluation shows that agents can handle pre-existing phishing emails safely yet remain susceptible to attacks adapted to agent behavior, while in an AgentPhishing evaluation of nine agents, four exhibit phishing-detection rates below $10\%$ and malicious-request compliance rates above $45\%$. These results highlight the limits of inferring agent safety from conventional phishing evaluations and the need to assess how agents respond to persuasive malicious requests.

Modern datacenters must balance three objectives that often conflict: keeping hardware within safe thermal limits, meeting latency expectations for high-priority work, and reducing the cost and carbon footprint of electricity. Traditional controllers handle these with fixed rules or heavily engineered optimization pipelines. This paper presents Grid Control, an autonomous datacenter orchestration system in which a large language model (LLM) acts as the decision-making agent. A simulated multi-region datacenter (5 regions, 15 servers, 60 chipsets) streams telemetry every second. Every decision interval the agent receives a frozen telemetry window and selects exactly one action from a small, closed vocabulary: shift_within_server, shift_within_region, migrate_region, or pass. A prioritized policy ranks overheating first, latency and load balance second, and cost and carbon third. Safety is enforced outside the model by a guardrail layer that routes high-criticality or administratorprohibited actions to a human approval queue. A feedback loop returns measured outcomes of past actions to the prompt as incontext learning signal, and a scope-restricted explainability module answers operator questions about the agent's behavior. Over 20 paired simulation runs, a deterministic stand-in for the agent's policy reduced time spent above the 68 °C threshold by about 24% and carbon-weighted load by about 9% relative to a no-agent baseline, with about 3% lower electricity cost. LLM-inthe-loop evaluation is left to future work. The contribution is an architecture and a reproducible testbed for studying safe, explainable, LLM-driven infrastructure control.

AI together with computational tools has completely changed the process of drug development because these technologies solve major issues that affect traditional methods which require long durations and high expenses and result in low success rates. The AI-driven techniques of virtual screening and molecular dynamics simulations and machine learning provide scientists with a method to discover targets and optimize leads and predict toxicity which they can use instead of traditional trial-and-error methods. The process receives further improvements from AI agents, who provide automated hypothesis generation and better chemical selection together with the ability to combine different types of biomedical information. They contribute significantly to clinical trials by performing patient stratification and implementing adaptive design and conducting real-time safety monitoring. The research field currently needs to overcome several obstacles because researchers require high-quality data, interpretable models, and extensive computational resources.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract This chapter examines how artificial intelligence transforms personal data processing and creates compliance challenges for organizations using predictive, generative, and agentic systems. It outlines the UK GDPR, the Data Protection Act 2018, the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, regulatory guidance, and the EU AI Act. The chapter analyses lawful bases, automated decision-making, training data acquisition, transparency, explainability, data subject rights, workplace monitoring, and governance responsibilities associated with AI deployment. It also addresses synthetic media, harmful content, cybersecurity risks, international transfers, procurement obligations, risk mitigation measures, and accountability standards for autonomous systems in public and private sector contexts. Finally, the chapter emphasizes practical compliance through impact assessments, privacy notices, vendor oversight, technical safeguards, organizational controls, and structured AI governance frameworks.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This systematic review investigated the medical potential of using artificial intelligence (AI) and holograms to improve body image as a means of maintaining sustainable and healthy beauty in the era of the longevity revolution. Although this review is a systematic review, it was conducted by individually setting related keywords according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-analyses (PRISMA) 2020 flowchart guidelines. The search method was as follows: PubMed, Google Scholar, Scopus and IEEE Xplore were searched with the keywords “longevity revolution,” “artificial intelligence,” “Customized beauty device,” “Customized Cosmetics,”, “body image,” “hologram,” “hologram health,” “AI hologram,” and “healthy body image.” Accordingly, a total of 11,117 articles were searched. In the final stage, 56 articles were selected and included in the paper. The results of this study suggest that the world is moving towards the longevity revolution era due to the development of biotechnology, genetic engineering, and medicine, and that healthy beauty is needed in response to this. In addition, the development and use of AI and holograms in the medical field are continuing, suggesting the possibility of using them for obesity and body shape health management diet management. Therefore, this represents the AI domain of sustainable human security. It suggests the future necessity of developing personalized physical health management utilizing AI and holograms, as well as the infinite potential of customized beauty devices and cosmetics.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Technology and Human Factors in Education and Health

documents.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) gradually enters the teaching and research contexts of higher education institutions, university teachers’ different perceptions of AI may elicit different psychological responses. Drawing on the Job Demands–Resources model, this study examines the effects of AI Challenge Awareness and AI Threat Awareness on university teachers’ Work Stress, and further analyzes the moderating roles of Digital Literacy and Perceived Organizational Support. Using university teachers as the research subjects, 421 valid samples were obtained through a questionnaire survey, and hierarchical regression analysis was employed to test the research hypotheses. The results indicate that AI Challenge Awareness is significantly and negatively correlated with university teachers’ Work Stress, whereas AI Threat Awareness is significantly and positively correlated with Work Stress. Both Digital Literacy and Perceived Organizational Support significantly weaken the positive effect of AI Threat Awareness on Work Stress, but neither of their moderating effects on the relationship between AI Challenge Awareness and Work Stress reaches a significant level. The findings suggest that university teachers’ perceptions of AI do not merely manifest as a source of stress; rather, their effects depend on individuals’ different interpretations of the work-related changes brought about by AI. Compared with challenge-oriented perceptions, threat-oriented perceptions are more readily transformed into Work Stress, while Digital Literacy and Perceived Organizational Support can, to a certain extent, buffer the stress induced by threat-oriented perceptions. The conclusions of this study help to deepen the understanding of individual differences in university teachers’ psychological responses in the context of AI, and provide references for higher education institutions to optimize the AI application environment and improve teacher support measures.

Abstract: Factchecking is among the key mechanisms for addressing information disorder. In the context of the growing integration of artificial intelligence, particularly large language models, into the information environment, the need for reliable information is increasing while access to it is more challenging. Thus, generative artificial intelligence can be both – an asset and a risk to factcheckers. The present study aims to examine the extent to which Claude.ai and ChatGPT can factcheck claims in Bulgarian. The experiment was conducted using a free skill developed by Nauka.bg. The claims were selected from the “Verified” section of Factcheck.bg, the largest fact-checking platform in Bulgaria. Through comparative content analysis, the study found that in most cases both models correctly identify false claims in accordance with Factcheck.bg’s publications. Claude.ai demonstrates a more authoritative tone and provides concise explanations supporting its verdicts. ChatGPT is more hesitant but offers greater detail, precision, and clarity in its explanations. Notably, ChatGPT rarely references its sources, whereas Claude.ai occasionally links to unreliable sources. A positive trend is Claude.ai’s note to consult official factchecking organizations and verified information sources.The results confirm the hypothesis that artificial intelligence can assist factcheckers but cannot replace human expertise in the verification process. Keywords: disinformation, factchecking, artificial intelligence, large language models, ChatGPT, Claude.ai.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Scientific research usually begins with a question, followed by a review of existing work, the development of possible The reasons for this, the planning of the experiments or simulations, and a careful verification of the results. Now artificial intelligence (AI) is being used can be used to help with a number of these steps. Large language models (LLMs) assist researchers in working with scientific information, AI agents can Tasks can be carried out using external tools, and evolutionary methods can continuously generate and test programs. The paper looks at four studies. that look at different parts of AI-assisted discovery: the wider influence of AI on science, autonomous agent systems, the TeLLAgent and the use of large language models in the search for evolutionary programming. Together, these studies demonstrate how AI could be of assistance with literature reviews and idea generation. They also highlight important issues, such as incorrect model outputs, and involve generation, computational testing, and program improvement. data that is biased or incomplete, the limited ability to generalize, poor reproducibility, reliance on tools, and data leakage that occurs during evaluation. The The paper examines the four studies and suggests a possible workflow for using AI responsibly in scientific research. Overall, AI can be It is a useful research assistant, but its suggestions have to be checked by way of transparent analysis and independent validation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: A system does not have to remove choice in order to shape it. It can define the problem, structure the options that appear, and create conditions under which a voluntary choice becomes costly to reverse. These mechanisms predate artificial intelligence. This paper asks what changes when AI-mediated systems operate them at greater speed, scale, and adaptability, and when the people subject to them cannot practically inspect, contest, or leave. The paper develops a four-part lens (problem definition, choice architecture, dependency formation, reversibility) and distinguishes institutional dependency from epistemic dependency. It adds an agency and accountability audit of six questions: who sets the objective, who controls the data, model and infrastructure, who can inspect the evidence, who bears the cost of error, who can override or replace the system, and what alternatives remain. Its central hypothesis, an accountability asymmetry, is stated with the evidence that would weaken it. A rubric scores safeguards by whether they have been exercised, not merely documented, and is applied to three current arrangements: the Robodebt scheme, the Medicare WISeR model, and the UnitedHealth nH Predict litigation. Where public evidence allows no score, the gap is reported as a finding. Appendices provide a one-page citizen audit card and a legal and case status snapshot as of 21 October 2026. This is a working paper. It has not been peer reviewed and is not legal advice. Claims are labelled documented, reported, interpretation, or hypothesis. The rubric is unvalidated and was scored by a single rater from public sources. Companion to Johnson (2026a) and Johnson (2026b).
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming drug discovery and pharmacology by enabling data-driven, predictive, and system-level approaches across the drug development lifecycle. This chapter provides a comprehensive overview of how machine learning, deep learning, graph neural networks, and generative AI are applied to target identification, molecular design, pharmacokinetics, ADMET prediction, and drug safety assessment. Emphasis is placed on the integration of multi-omics data, systems pharmacology, and explainable AI to enhance mechanistic understanding and regulatory relevance. The chapter also examines real-world case studies, ethical considerations, and evolving regulatory perspectives, highlighting challenges related to data quality, bias, and validation. Overall, it presents a forward-looking roadmap for responsible, regulatory-grade AI adoption in pharmacological research and drug development.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Introduction Positive and negative attitudes toward artificial intelligence (AI) may have partly distinct psychological correlates. This cross-sectional study examined whether AI anxiety statistically accounted for associations between AI literacy and positive and negative attitudes toward AI among preservice teachers. Methods Participants were 335 preservice teachers enrolled in a faculty of education in Türkiye. Data were collected using the Artificial Intelligence Literacy Scale, Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale, Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale, and a personal information form. Two indirect-effect models were estimated using PROCESS Model 4 with 5,000 bootstrap resamples, controlling for prior AI training. Results AI literacy was negatively associated with AI anxiety and positively associated with positive attitudes toward AI. AI anxiety was positively associated with negative attitudes but was not significantly associated with positive attitudes. The indirect association through AI anxiety was significant for negative attitudes but not for positive attitudes, and a direct bootstrap contrast confirmed that the two indirect effects differed significantly (B = −0.118, 95% CI [−0.201, −0.039]). Prior AI training was not significantly associated with either attitude dimension. A sensitivity analysis excluding the three reverse-worded AI literacy items reproduced this pattern. Discussion The findings indicate that positive and negative attitudes toward AI may have partly distinct psychological correlates: AI literacy is directly related to positive evaluations, whereas its association with negative evaluations is statistically linked to AI anxiety. Because the data are cross-sectional, the indirect effects should not be interpreted as evidence of causal mediation.

AI PCs and on-device artificial intelligence are changing how everyday computers use AI. Instead of sending every request to a remote cloud server, a device can process suitable tasks locally using its CPU, GPU, and specialised neural processing unit (NPU). This can reduce response time, limit data transfer, support some functions without a stable internet connection, and give users more control over personal data. The practical value of these benefits depends on the task, the model, and the computer's hardware. Local processing also has to work within limits such as memory capacity, power consumption, heat, and model size. This review discusses three research works: a comprehensive survey of on-device AI models, a study proposing a collaborative consumer edge-AI ecosystem, and research on on-device AI for smart environments and Industry 4.0. The papers are compared by focus, approach, contribution, and limitation. The review identifies model optimisation, efficient hardware use, privacy-aware collaboration, and energy management as important areas. It also finds that the selected works do not establish a common benchmark specifically for AI PCs. A task-aware local/cloud architecture is proposed for future study; it has not been experimentally tested.

Live-streaming plays a vital role in tourism product marketing. Consumers often struggle to obtain sufficient product information through live-streaming, leading to information asymmetry and low trust, which hinder transaction efficiency. To address these challenges, an increasing number of live-streaming platforms are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) services to help consumers better understand tourism products. However, investment in AI services requires substantial financial resources, while suppliers’ information disclosure directly affects the transparency of tourism product information. A Stackelberg game model examines how government regulation and financing strategies shape supplier information disclosure, platform AI investment, and supply chain profits. The results show the following: (1) The platform’s financing choice is not determined solely by financing costs. The relative advantage of supplier financing over bank financing depends jointly on relative financing rates, consumers’ sensitivity to AI services, and the platform’s altruistic preference; (2) Neither strategy dominates. Subsidies are more advantageous when reward-and-penalty intensity is low, whereas reward-and-penalty regulation becomes preferable as the intensity increases. (3) Platform altruism boosts AI investment and supplier profit but may reduce platform profit when commissions are low or consumers are less AI-sensitive. These findings provide theoretical guidance for live-streaming platforms to optimize their financing and AI service investment decisions, and for governments to design differentiated information disclosure regulations.

Purpose This research examines when and why artificial intelligence (AI) source disclosure reduces participation in sustainable advertising. It proposes that AI source disclosure is associated with lower felt obligation toward the campaign organization and that this negative effect depends on appeal type and decision-making orientation. Design/methodology/approach Five experiments tested the proposed model. Study 1 used an interactive webpage and a consequential sharing task to examine actual participation. Study 2 examined felt obligation as the proposed mediator while testing perceived sincerity as an alternative explanation. Studies 3 and 4 tested the moderating role of warmth versus competence appeals in Chinese and US samples, respectively. Study 5 examined instrumental versus normative decision-making as an additional boundary condition. Findings Campaigns attributed to AI sources generated lower participation than campaigns attributed to human sources. This effect was associated with reduced felt obligation toward the organization, while sincerity and authenticity were not supported as mediators. The negative effect was stronger for warmth appeals and normative decision-making, but weaker for competence appeals and instrumental decision-making. Originality/value This research identifies felt obligation toward the campaign organization as a pathway associated with responses to AI source disclosure in sustainable advertising. It extends the stereotype content model by demonstrating that appeal type conditions the AI source-disclosure effect and contributes to stakeholder and AI decision-making research by identifying decision-making orientation as an additional boundary condition.

Consider the following scenarios: A student unhappy with a grade cites three federal regulations and a circuit court opinion in an email to a professor. An employee facing a corrective action plan submits a two‐page rebuttal organized by legal elements, complete with case citations. A community member follows up an open‐records request with a follow‐up letter quoting the statute's response deadline down to the business day. None of these individuals has ever consulted an attorney. All of them have an artificial intelligence partner open in another tab.

This chapter examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can be integrated into business training and development (T&D) to strengthen organizational capacity for long-term viability. Drawing on action learning, experiential learning, and enterprise education, it outlines how AI-enabled tools, such as intelligent coaching systems, adaptive feedback mechanisms, and decision-support platforms, can support the development of transversal capabilities, including systemic thinking, problem-solving, and decision-making. The analysis adopts a design perspective, advancing an architecture for AI-augmented training that connects educational and workplace contexts. Strategic considerations are proposed for creating individualized and scalable learning environments that address the dual imperative of workforce development and organizational adaptability under complex, evolving conditions. The chapter integrates pedagogical models and systems design principles to offer a coherent framework for embedding AI in organizational T&D.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Air pollution is a major environmental concern because it affects human health, ecosystems, and the quality of life in urban and industrial areas. Traditional monitoring systems often depend on fixed stations and manual sampling. Although these methods provide useful measurements, they may have high operating costs, limited spatial coverage, and delays in reporting. Recent developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), the Internet of Things (IoT), and wireless sensors offer ways to monitor air quality continuously and forecast pollution levels. This review examines four supplied papers covering AI and ML models with wireless sensors, IoT-based monitoring, comparisons between traditional and AI-based methods, and a proposed smart-city forecasting framework. The reviewed literature describes applications such as missing-data estimation, sensor calibration, anomaly detection, Air Quality Index (AQI) estimation, and short-term pollution forecasting. Models including regression, Random Forest, Support Vector Machines, neural networks, and deep-learning methods are discussed. The papers also identify challenges related to data quality, sensor reliability, cost, scalability, model transfer between locations, and system integration. One proposed framework reports improved prediction results, but these figures are treated as results reported by that paper rather than independently verified findings. Overall, AI can support earlier warnings and better-informed pollution management when it is combined with reliable sensors , quality data, and local validation.

This paper provides a comprehensive review of the convergence of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital twin (DT) technologies in advanced predictive maintenance (PdM) in modern industrial ecosystems. Traditional maintenance strategies (from reactive maintenance to planned preventive maintenance) often do not account for random degradation patterns, resulting in unplanned equipment downtime or unnecessary operating expenses. By combining real-time Internet of Things (IoT) multi-sensor telemetry streams with high-fidelity physical information and data-driven virtual replicas, AI-powered digital twins provide continuous health monitoring, immediate anomaly isolation and accurate Remaining Useful Life (RUL) calculation. This paper systematically reviews key architectural frameworks, machine learning and deep learning paradigms, edge-cloud deployment topologies, prominent industrial challenges, and future research avenues in Industry 4.0.

This project presents an AI-Based Home Energy Monitoring with automated load system designed to monitor and manage household electricity consumption ,efficiently ,ON/OFF controlling sysyem. The system uses voltage and current sensors to measure real-time electrical parameters to provide values of current and voltage to calculate the power value, which are processed and transmitted using an ESP32 microcontroller. The microcontroller will process the data in into computer singles data .The collected data is stored in a database for continuous tracking and evaluation. Artificial intelligence techniques are applied to analyze household energy habits, forecast future power usage, estimate electricity costs, and highlight instances of unnecessary energy waste. To take proactive action, the system integrates a six-channel relay module that can automatically switch specific appliance loads on or off based on predicted energy trends and preset safety conditions. A web-based dashboard is provided to display real-time usage data, load statuses, billing estimates, and system alerts. Overall, the system offers a practical and low-cost solution for real-time monitoring and automated load management in smart homes.

The rapid growth of digital messaging means that information reaches large audiences but has also led to the circulation of false, misleading, manipulated, and unverified claims.WhatsApp-style messages pose particular challenges because they are often short, informal, forwarded without context, and written in English, Hindi, or Hinglish.This paper proposes an artificial intelligence (AI)-based framework for the detection and classification of potentially misleading information in WhatsApp-style messages using Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Machine Learning (ML) to detect and classify such messages.The framework comprises dataset preparation, text preprocessing, feature extraction, model training, message classification, warning generation, and performance evaluation.Candidate approaches include TF-IDF with traditional classifiers and contextual representations from transformer-based models.Messages are expected to be assigned to four categories: Reliable, Misinformation, Misleading, and Unverified.The evaluation plan uses accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, macro-F1, and a confusion matrix.As this work describes a proposed research framework, no experimental performance results are claimed.The system is designed as an early-warning and decision-support mechanism rather than a replacement for human factchecking.

Portable Document Format (PDF) files are the most common way of storing reports, research papers, manuals, and legal documents, but their layout-oriented structure makes them difficult to search and to query conversationally. Large Language Models (LLMs) can answer questions fluently, but they may hallucinate and cannot process long documents that exceed a fixed context window. This study presents the design, implementation, and preliminary testing of a PDF chat and summarization system based on Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The system uses a three-stage data pipeline (raw, processed, and RAG-ready) that parses PDFs, removes repeating headers and footers, converts content to Markdown, and applies structure-aware chunking, which attaches section-path metadata to every chunk. Answers are generated by the openai/gpt-oss-120b model (served through the Groq API) using passages retrieved from a local ChromaDB vector store with all-MiniLM-L6-v2 sentence embeddings, and are returned with page references. Three chunking strategies (fixed-size, Markdown-aware, and hierarchical) are defined, and an evaluation protocol based on answer accuracy, faithfulness, hit rate at k, unsupported-answer rate, and response time is specified for comparing them. In preliminary testing, the system processed uploaded PDFs and answered natural-language questions with an average response time of approximately 2–5 seconds. A full comparative evaluation is left for future work. The study provides a reproducible, small-scale baseline that student and small-team developers can extend, and it argues that document preprocessing and chunking quality are central to the reliability of PDF question answering

Digital documents, paraphrasing tools and large language models have made plagiarism much harder to catch than plain copy-and-paste matching. This review looks at five research papers that approach academic plagiarism detection from different directions: a systematic literature survey, text-based feature selection, deep learning, a comparison of detection techniques, and the detection of AI-obfuscated plagiarism in modeling assignments. Between them, the studies draw on lexical overlap, sentence structure, semantic similarity, writing style and token sequences taken from structured modeling artifacts. One study pairs Chi-square feature selection with a Support Vector Machine (SVM) and reports F-measure scores of 89.34% on PAN 2013 and 92.95% on PAN 2014; another reports that its LSTM-based system placed first among the systems it was compared with on the same benchmarks. A more recent approach for modeling assignments normalizes tokens, matches them automatically and leaves the final judgement to a human inspector, which makes it more resistant to AI-based obfuscation. Taken together, the papers show that no single similarity measure can handle every kind of plagiarism. A practical AI-based checker should therefore combine fast candidate retrieval, several text and structure features, carefully validated machine-learning models and human review. Open problems include resistance to paraphrasing, coverage of datasets and languages, fair evaluation, and the danger of reading a detector score as conclusive proof.

Cow shelters need coordination between animal identification, health observations, activity tracking, environmental factors, feed and water supplies, vaccination schedules, medical records, and operational actions. Precision livestock farming has created useful tools using sensors, identification systems and artificial intelligence. Recent reviews still show problems with combining information, checking data quality, making systems work together, and supporting decisions [1] [2] [7] [10] [24]. This paper introduces a cow-shelter system that connects RFID animal tagging, different types of IoT sensors, ESP32-based data collection at the edge, Wi-Fi communication, Flask web services, MySQL databases, clear rule-based alerts, and machine learning—all within a single management process. The system links animal data with shelter-zone details and keeps track of time, data quality, management actions, and past alerts. The analysis is done in stages: simple rules give alerts, and machine learning comes later once enough labelled and checked data is available. Features used in the analysis include sensor readings, changes over time, average trends, activity summaries, environmental data, and feed and water status. A repeatable way to test the system is created, measuring sensing delay, alert timing, data transmission reliability, dashboard speed, recovery after failure, and how well predictions work. The main contribution is not in technology but in the full system design: an information-to-action process built around animal identity, multiple sensors, resource tracking, records, analysis, alerts, and human input. The paper does not give accuracy or timing results and does not claim the individual parts are new.

Digital twins are increasingly proposed as a means of linking aquatic observations, predictive models and management decisions. Their relevance to sustainability nevertheless depends on more than the speed or accuracy of an artificial intelligence model. This critical narrative review examines the evidence connecting digital-twin architectures with capture fisheries, aquaculture and freshwater and coastal water-quality monitoring. Literature published through 30 July 2026 was selected through targeted scholarly searches, citation tracing and bibliographic verification, with particular attention to observation quality, independent validation, operational feedback and management outcomes. The synthesis distinguishes a digital model, a continuously updated digital representation and a decision-linked twin, and separates component performance from demonstrated ecological benefit. Evidence supports advances in image-based monitoring, satellite retrievals, hybrid environmental prediction and selected field deployments. It is substantially less conclusive regarding sustained stock recovery, equitable allocation or ecosystem-scale benefits attributable to a complete digital-twin system. Important limitations include imperfect observability, inappropriate spatial and temporal validation, uncertain transfer between environments, simulator-dependent policy optimisation and incomplete treatment of human behaviour. Apparent disagreement between promising technical demonstrations and limited management evidence largely reflects different endpoints and system boundaries rather than a simple conflict over technological feasibility. A federated, decision-centred framework is proposed in which traceable observations support uncertainty-aware state estimation, explicit management objectives, constrained decision support and independently audited outcomes. The framework includes staged deployment, human authorisation, local data governance and lifecycle assessment; it is an unvalidated synthesis rather than an implemented system. Near-term priorities are prospective forecasting benchmarks, comparative management trials, failure-tolerant monitoring and participatory evaluation in data-limited fisheries. Digital twins are most defensible as accountable extensions of existing environmental observation and adaptive management, not as substitutes for ecological understanding, enforceable institutions or legitimate collective decisions.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is a nascent technology that could become a general-purpose technology and can have significant impacts on economic development, productivity growth, labour markets and good governance. The study will delve into the potential impact of Artificial Intelligence on the economy and job landscape of India as part of the vision of Viksit Bharat by 2047. The study uses qualitative review-based research methodology that is based on analyzing evidence from the academic literature, government documents, as well as reports produced by national and international institutions. AI has the potential to augment productivity, innovate solutions, modernize industries, contribute to digital governance and create job opportunities, as revealed by this study. At the same time, the implementation of AI can be challenging due to the changes in labor markets, lack of skills, digital divide, fragility of the informal sector, data privacy and security concerns, algorithmic biases, and institutional preparedness. In this study, it is argued that AI will not necessarily take the place of jobs, but rather change the employment type if suitable reskilling measures are taken. It identifies the following policy priorities – human capital, digital infrastructure, responsible AI governance, research and innovation, and social protection.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Project management requires coordination of tasks, deadlines, dependencies, resources, and risks. Manual status reporting and inconsistent prioritisation can make emerging delivery problems difficult to identify. This paper proposes and demonstrates a framework connecting task prioritisation, progress monitoring, and task-delay risk identification. The framework combines transparent rule-based scoring, monitoring flags, a machine-learning classifier, and human review. A prototype was evaluated using 1,000 generated task records, with a Decision Tree compared against a majority-class baseline on a held-out test set. The Decision Tree achieved 61.0% accuracy, 27.4% precision, 57.5% recall, and an F1-score of 37.1% for the delay class. The baseline achieved 80.0% accuracy but detected no delayed tasks, demonstrating why accuracy alone can be misleading in imbalanced classification. These results describe the prototype experiment and do not establish effectiveness on real project records. The paper concludes that an integrated framework can provide a reproducible basis for further evaluation, with real-world validation required before operational use. Keywords: artificial intelligence, project management automation, task prioritisation, progress monitoring, risk identification, delay prediction, Decision Tree, business analytics

Accelerated progress in digital technologies has influenced all industries. Interest in embracing Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education and research is flourishing among scholars, practitioners, educators, students, and the general public. Educational institutions now need to transform their traditional approach towards teaching and research by implementing innovative technologies. However, controversies surrounding the use of AI in education or research require deeper examination. Moreover, integration sustainability in business education has become an obligation for universities around the world. The significance of universities in empowering generations to tackle complex sustainability issues calls for ground-breaking solutions. In this regard, AI with its immense capabilities can offer a unique approach. This chapter aims to explore AI trends and tendencies in teaching and research and to shed light on the role of AI in sustainability education. The main research question is: How can AI be incorporated into teaching to enhance sustainability education? To achieve research aims, the qualitative research method was used and expert interview approach was applied. This research contributes to the discussion of introducing AI in sustainability education and research agenda by delving into the multifaceted intersection of AI, sustainability and education. Based on the results, a theoretical framework is proposed to adopt AI into sustainable development teaching. The findings benefit academics, educators, researchers, policymakers and industry representatives to grasp future trends in sustainability education through AI-powered initiatives.

Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are transforming disaster management through intelligent decision support, predictive resource allocation, and adaptive operational planning. Volunteer management — a critical yet underexplored challenge in humanitarian logistics — represents a domain where AI-driven optimization can deliver substantial operational gains. This chapter presents a three-stage AI-enabled decision support framework for volunteer allocation in large-scale disaster response. At its core is a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) model that constitutes the optimization layer of a broader AI-assisted humanitarian logistics ecosystem. The model assigns volunteers to disaster management centers while maximizing demand satisfaction, respecting capacity and travel-time constraints, incorporating individual preferences, enforcing group cohesion to improve long-term retention, and preventing scheduling conflicts. Computational experiments using a synthetic scenario with 100 volunteers, six volunteer types, four disaster management centers, and a seven-day response horizon confirm the model’s feasibility: the MILP solver reaches a solution in under 8 seconds and generates schedules that substantially reduce unmet demand. Sensitivity analysis on the preference–demand trade-off reveals important operational dynamics. The chapter concludes with a roadmap for extending the framework with machine learning demand forecasting, reinforcement learning-based dynamic reassignment, digital twin simulation, and predictive retention modeling — positioning the system as a foundation for next-generation AI tools in disaster humanitarian logistics.

This review examines the various ways artificial intelligence (AI) can influence school management and its potential to promote sustainable education. It brings together the findings from earlier studies to illustrate how schools are using AI to simplify administrative tasks, enrich learning experiences, and support sustainable education efforts. Key uses include AI tools for real-time data analysis, better resource management, and personalised learning paths that connect students with real-world environmental issues. By managing tasks such as data cleaning and report generation, AI enables educators and staff to dedicate more time to strategic initiatives like developing curricula and engaging the community in sustainability projects. The review also highlights major challenges and risks of using AI in education, such as concerns about data privacy, the need for reliable infrastructure, and ethical issues related to algorithmic bias. The findings show that although AI provides powerful tools for creating efficient and environmentally conscious schools, successful and fair implementation requires careful planning, targeted teacher training, and a focus on equal access. The article concludes by emphasising key areas for future research, underlining the need for robust frameworks to enable schools to use AI responsibly while promoting both academic excellence and a culture of sustainability and sustainable education.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: This study seeks to elucidate how the higher education systems of China and Japan have addressed the issue of plagiarism exacerbated by generative artificial intelligence (AIGC-plagiarism) and the insights gained from these responses. As generative AI becomes increasingly integrated with higher education, the age-old problem of plagiarism has resurfaced with greater intensity and elusiveness, sweeping across universities worldwide. Although no definitive consensus exists regarding the precise definition of AIGC-plagiarism, this conceptual ambiguity does not preclude its broad recognition as prohibited academic conduct. The relationship between cutting-edge technologies and higher education appears to have reached an impasse, yet the majority of Chinese institutions have maintained a stance of silence, while the Chinese government has shown concern but refrained from taking formal action. This research comparatively examines the response strategies to AIGC-plagiarism by the Japanese government and 359 universities, which share similar systemic and institutional contexts with their Chinese counterparts, and reaches a conclusion that the practice of “No Copy + Exceptions” emerges as a particularly instructive approach. A micro-level comparative analysis reveals that this regulatory inertia is shaped by both technological and political factors, and represents a pragmatic strategy in the face of technological uncertainty. Regardless of the underlying rationale, such silence constitutes an unacceptable form of de facto endorsement or passive acquiescence. Higher education systems must develop more proactive, responsive, and agile mechanisms to cultivate morally anchored, innovation-capable students amidst technological and geopolitical turbulence. Key components of this mechanism include, but are not limited to a unified national benchmark and implementation rule, a dynamic AI impact assessment structure, autonomy of faculty and academic councils, and student participation with feedback channels.

Formal on-demand online courses offer professionals a structured way to acquire knowledge that is relevant to their work, and can complement workplace learning. However, connecting between such formal learning and work brings two essential challenges: (1) identifying and articulating work-grounded learning objectives and mapping them to formal learning; and (2) transferring knowledge newly acquired in the learning space to the workplace. Reflection, guided by AI tools, may be a useful way to support these processes. This chapter first frames reflective practice as a way of working—with continuous reflection alongside work—and then presents three cases where AI-guided reflection bridged formal learning and work. In a socio-technical design space, AI tools can prompt and structure reflection, provide feedback, and offer data analytics as a “looking glass” on work practice. In doing so, they steer attention and shape how professionals reflect. At the same time, professionals retain agency to choose, configure, and use tools; but professionals’ competence is a pre-requisite for effective such reflective practice. Subsequently, our vision for technology-oriented research is to further develop systems that (1) facilitate the articulation of learning needs, (2) facilitate knowledge transfer by using rich and multimodal evidence from the workplace to support AI-guided reflection, and (3) expand interaction affordances towards more situated and embodied AI-guidance (e.g., multimodal sensing and analytics, ambient prompts, voice-first coaching, agentic companions) that may better fit workplace constraints and ways of working, and (4) help professionals further develop their agency in reflective practice through such hybrid, multimodal and embodied AI. In parallel, a challenge for workplace learning-oriented research is to examine AI-guidance in-situ and to develop socio-technical AI design patterns, as combinations of technology design and usage. Formal on-demand learning providers are uniquely positioned to take up such AI-guidance as part of their offerings, with a recommendation to provide both tools and training in using tools, and teaching, coaching, and mentoring to build professionals’ reflection competence.
topics: Human Resource Development and Performance Evaluation

documents.abstract: Ethical, scientific and translational limitations of animal testing have increased the global pursuit of high quality, human relevant, biomedical research, toxicological, and drug development alternatives. The combination of artificial intelligence (AI) and cell-based assays, organ-on-chip (OoC) technologies, and computational modelling, is transforming the paradigm of experimental research by promoting predictive, scalable, and ethically responsible research. The chapter gives a general but inclusionary review of AI-based substitutes of animal testing in reference to three pillars of change, including advanced cell-based systems, micro physiological organ-on-chip technology, and AI-enabled virtual bodies (in silico models).The chapter starts with the analysis of the historical dependence on animal models, regulatory/ethical forces behind replacing, minimizing, and refining (3Rs).

This chapter analyzes how artificial intelligence (AI) and nano-drones can be used as a revolutionary method to make agriculture sustainable. It presents new AI-drone architects that can target two fundamental uses: the precision control of pests and automated waste valorization. We show how high-resolution optical and multispectral sensors on AI-enabled nano-drones can provide an early warning of pests and eco-friendly pesticide control by reducing chemical use. We discuss the contribution of an AI-based waste valorization system in which nano-drones automatically detect, classify, and harvest farm waste to be converted into bioenergy and organic fertilizers. A machine-learning algorithm allows these drones to predict waste types and optimize downstream processes. The chapter also outlines real-time monitoring of crops using drone sensors to measure health levels of plants, soil nutrients, and irrigation requirements to provide predictive analytics to optimize crop yields. Critical issues such as regulatory frameworks, data privacy, and infrastructure shortcomings, which need to be overcome for deployment at scale, are discussed. The chapter provides a data-driven, automation-focused framework to AI-enabled nano-drones in sustainable agriculture.

Airway image analysis systems play an increasingly important role in computer-assisted diagnosis, quantitative airway assessment, intervention planning, and respiratory disease management. However, the development of robust airway analysis methods remains challenging due to the complex geometry of airway structures, strong class imbalance, variability in imaging protocols, and the need to preserve anatomical connectivity across multiple spatial scales. Recent advances in topology-aware learning, transformer-based architectures, and foundation-model adaptation have substantially changed the landscape of airway image analysis, motivating an updated review focused specifically on airway-oriented systems. In this narrative review, we provide a comprehensive overview of the datasets, evaluation methodologies, and computational approaches that underpin modern airway image analysis systems. We discuss the imaging modalities and publicly available datasets commonly used for airway analysis and examine their strengths, limitations, and implications for algorithm development and benchmarking. Particular attention is given to evaluation methodologies, including overlap-based, surface-distance, and topology-aware metrics that assess both segmentation accuracy and structural correctness. We further review the evolution of computational approaches, covering convolutional neural networks, transformer-based architectures, hybrid methods, topology-aware and tubular-aware networks, foundation-model adaptations, and data-efficient learning strategies. Finally, we discuss current challenges related to dataset availability, annotation quality, model generalization, topology preservation, and clinical deployment, and outline future research directions toward robust, interpretable, and clinically deployable airway image analysis systems.

Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) has become an important research direction because intelligent systems are increasingly used to support decisions in complex and uncertain environments. However, the interpretability of a decision depends not only on the final prediction but also on the mathematical structure through which the prediction is obtained. This paper develops an algebraic framework for interpretable multi-criteria decision-making based on bounded ordered structures, weighted aggregation, and explicit criterion-level contributions. A finite set of alternatives is evaluated using normalized criteria, and a weighted score is assigned to each alternative. The framework represents criterion values in a bounded lattice and uses an order-preserving aggregation operator to obtain transparent rankings. Mathematical properties concerning monotonicity, boundedness, score decomposition, and stability under perturbations are established. An illustrative numerical example involving the selection of an artificial intelligence model demonstrates how the framework generates rankings and human-readable explanations. The approach provides a mathematically explicit foundation for decision support and can be extended to fuzzy, linguistic, and neutrosophic environments. The proposed framework and numerical example are illustrative; novelty and performance claims require literature verification and empirical validation. Keywords: Abstract algebra; lattice theory; explainable artificial intelligence; multi-criteria decision-making; interpretable decision systems; weighted aggregation.

The fast adoption of Artificial Intelligence in the child-facing digital ecosystem has changed marketing into a reactive personalization model to a predictive and pre-emptive model of shaping choice. This chapter envisions an algorithmic childhood futures, in which AI technologies predict preferences and restructure the choice environment of children prior to the desire developing consciously. Based on the interdisciplinary theory and the latest case studies provided in the educational platforms and smart toy ecosystems, the chapter proves how predictive architectures may promote engagement and gradually reduce exploration and redistribute agency. This analysis puts the concept of algorithmic influence in a new perspective, as temporal harm, with its long-term developmental consequences, that are still poorly dealt with in existing governance models. To create a balance between innovation, commercial goals and digital well-being, the chapter ends with the suggestions to child-centered design and managerial principles.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence promises to democratize personalized tutoring, yet the longitudinal stability of adaptive systems remains under-theorized. Current ethical discourse focuses on static bias. This paper argues that a distinct threat lies in algorithmic drift: a feedback loop in which minor, demographically asymmetric observation errors compound over time into systemic inequities. We make three contributions. First, we formalize algorithmic drift as a coupled learner--tutor dynamical system. Second, we corroborate this theory with an agent-based Monte Carlo simulation in which either a transparent online tracker or an LSTM deep-knowledge-tracing network drives an IRT-based curriculum policy. Third, we introduce the temporal fairness stabilizer (TFS), a targeted intervention that periodically re-probes learner capability, and benchmark it against standard exploration baselines with explicit group-fairness metrics and replication-level inference. Within the modeled environment, TFS closes the achievement gap where generic exploration does not, and we characterize the conditions under which it succeeds. We separate what is established analytically, what is demonstrated in simulation, and what remains to be validated with real learners. Our results reframe algorithmic fairness in education as a temporal property of a closed loop rather than a deployment-time checkbox.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning
Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This phenomenological study explores the lived experiences of Thai Generation Z hikers, thoroughly examining the critical intersection of artificial intelligence (AI) literacy and complex decision-making in wilderness environments. As young adventurers increasingly pursue nature-based eco-experientia for psychological restoration, AI has rapidly evolved into an active, front-facing backcountry companion. Using the Theory of Technological Mediation alongside robust methodological triangulation—including in-depth interviews, focus groups, and interactive discussions with university-aged hikers—this research examines how algorithmic tools profoundly reshape human-nature relationships. The empirical findings clearly show that AI is seamlessly integrated throughout the trekking lifecycle, functioning as a vital digital safety net that mitigates environmental uncertainty. However, this deep integration precipitates a highly complex socio-technical paradox. While participants consistently exhibit exceptional functional AI literacy, an emerging algorithmic dependency actively threatens to erode traditional, intuitive wilderness judgment. Ultimately, AI facilitates a hermeneutic relationship in which pristine nature is interpreted through curated data, fundamentally transforming raw exploration into a mediated digital reality that urgently requires careful preservation of human agency within adventure tourism.

The increasing demand for large annotated datasets in computer vision underscores the need for scalable synthetic data generation methods, as traditional approaches often lack adaptability or offer limited annotations. To address these challenges, this work introduces a comprehensive methodology that leverages 3D Gaussian splatting and Blender to generate photorealistic synthetic datasets with automatic annotations, suitable for training deep learning computer vision models in multiple tasks, including object detection, pose estimation, semantic and instance segmentation, depth estimation, and surface normal estimation. Designed for broad applicability, this approach was developed with the significant challenges of industrial scenarios in mind, where data scarcity impedes the development of resilient AI-based situational awareness systems. The proposed pipeline can model any target scenario by reconstructing high-fidelity 3D environments, integrating synthetic objects through diverse modeling techniques, and applying procedural generation to vary lighting, camera angles, and object placements. With all annotations generated automatically, this approach facilitates the efficient creation of extensive annotated datasets, thereby eliminating manual labeling efforts. To validate the effectiveness of our synthetic data, we train computer vision models exclusively on these datasets and evaluate their performance in real applications, demonstrating their generalization capability and practical relevance. The results confirm that our methodology provides a scalable, flexible, and high-quality alternative to traditional data collection, bridging the gap between synthetic and real-world datasets while offering a powerful tool for both research and industrial applications. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/juanjesus-ldo/scene_generator .

Technology tools used for professional upskilling change on a timescale of weeks, and written guidance about them ages at the same pace. Large language models have made it inexpensive to draft a tutorial or a course outline, but most deployed generation systems still produce a piece of content once and never check it against what an audience actually does with it. This paper describes an agentic pipeline, organized as a typed workflow graph, that treats instructional content production as a manufacturing process with explicit checkpoints rather than a single generation call. Four node classes structure the graph: deterministic scripts, model steps bound to a fixed rubric, open-ended agent phases, and human approval gates, arranged along a forward production path and closed by a feedback cycle that rewrites generation rules from post level engagement telemetry. Production of content is split into two layers: a demand layer, built from video and community sources, that shapes topic selection and register, and an authority layer, built from official documentation, that every published claim must trace back to. Over five months of continuous operation, the deployed system published 26 documented guides at roughly 1.5 hours of operator time per week, and the feedback loop identified four measurable engagement effects that became binding rules for later runs, including a hook style that outperformed baseline by a factor of 1.83 in its first analysis window.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Knowledge graph-to-text (KG-to-text) generation verbalizes a set of knowledge graph triples into fluent natural language. While fine-tuned encoder-decoder models have long been the standard approach, recent LLMs are becoming increasingly competitive. We benchmark recent LLMs against fine-tuned encoder-decoder models, using reference-based metrics and graph-grounded reference-free LLM-based evaluation validated against human annotations. We observed that recent LLMs substantially narrow, and in several settings close, the gap with fine-tuned models on reference-based metrics, while performing better on graph-grounded metrics. LLM-based evaluation scores show limited correlation with reference-based metrics, suggesting that the two approaches capture different aspects of generation quality. Graph-grounded evaluation reveals that prompted models produce fewer contradictions and triple omissions than fine-tuned models, and these errors increase more rapidly with graph size for fine-tuned models, highlighting differences between the two approaches that reference-based metrics may not fully capture.

Despite sustained attention to patient safety, avoidable harm remains prevalent in acute and rehabilitation settings, often arising from communication failures, fragmented teamwork and limited situational awareness. Traditional safety mechanisms are largely reactive and do not consistently support real-time risk management. Focused clinical daily safety huddles (FCDSHs) have emerged as a proactive, nurse-led intervention to close this gap. FCDSHs are structured, multidisciplinary and action oriented, with a focus on identifying and mitigating avoidable patient safety risks. Effective implementation requires preparation, consistent facilitation, multidisciplinary engagement and psychological safety, supported by proportionate documentation and clear escalation processes. Nursing leadership is central to embedding and sustaining FCDSHs within routine clinical practice. Making FCDSHs part of routine care strengthens situational awareness and teamwork while proactively mitigating avoidable patient safety risks.

Background Teachers’ health and quality of life are important to school health and education policy. This study examined lifestyle behaviors, mental well-being, satisfaction, and health-related absence among female schoolteachers in Saudi Arabia. Methods A mixed-methods study in the Eastern Province combined a cross-sectional questionnaire completed by 562 female government-school teachers with semi-structured interviews with 19 teachers. Mental well-being was assessed using the WHO-5. Associations were examined using Spearman correlation and multivariable logistic regression. Interviews were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis with an inductive approach. Results Poor mental well-being (WHO-5 ≤ 50) was reported by 58.4% of teachers, and 24.4% scored ≤28. No moderate-intensity activity was reported by 42.3%; 77.4% of 561 respondents slept six hours or less. Unhealthy foods were consumed several times per week or almost daily by 52.5%; only 29.9% consumed fruit and vegetables daily. Poor or very poor sleep quality was reported by 19.4%, and tobacco use by 3.4%. Overall, 27.9% brushed their teeth less than twice daily, and 52.1% last visited a dentist over two years earlier. Tooth or gum pain at least sometimes during the preceding three months was reported by 61.9%. Sleep quality and duration showed moderate positive correlations with well-being ( r = 0.390 and 0.302, respectively; p < 0.001). Physical activity, dietary behaviors, toothbrushing, and oral pain were also associated with well-being. Higher teaching load was weakly associated with lower satisfaction ( r = −0.098, p = 0.020). Lifestyle and satisfaction scores remained associated with good well-being after adjustment (OR = 1.051, 95% CI: 1.030–1.073; and 1.035, 95% CI: 1.022–1.048, respectively). Self-rated health also remained associated with good well-being. Lower lifestyle and well-being scores were associated with more health-related absence (all p < 0.05). Five themes described demanding workdays, barriers to healthy routines, emotional strain, work extending into home life, and occupational health concerns. Conclusion Unhealthy daily routines and poor mental well-being were common among teachers. These findings support greater attention to teacher health in education policy. School health promotion should include manageable work demands, time for rest, and access to preventive care. Sustained investment in workplace health promotion may support teachers’ well-being and quality of life.

Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is the most common pediatric chronic inflammatory rheumatic condition, with substantial quality-of-life impacts. Treatment selection is complex due to limited guideline evidence, and difficult trade-offs. Decisions are often solely physician driven. We evaluated the feasibility of Large Language Model-based Decision Aid (LLM-DA) designed to support collaborative rather than solely physician decision-making in JIA care. A multi-method feasibility study was conducted in accordance with the TRIPOD-LLM checklist. The aims were twofold: first, to assess the quality of the LLM-DA (OpenAI’s o3 model) based on evaluations from three pediatric rheumatologists and an exploratory assessment by an LLM-as-a-Judge (OpenAI’s GPT-5 model); and second, to characterize perceived value of the tool from the patient perspective through a mixed methods evaluation (n = 34). For 10 de-identified use cases, rheumatologists and LLM-Judge generated treatment recommendations and scored the LLM-DA outputs on safety, factual consistency, treatment appropriateness, and preference acknowledgment. Rheumatologists rated 97% of outputs as acceptable for safety and preference acknowledgment, 60% for factual consistency, 70% for appropriateness. Treatment recommendation agreement among all evaluators and real-world data was low at <30%. Inter-rater agreement for scores among rheumatologists was almost perfect for safety and preference acknowledgement, moderate for treatment appropriateness, and poor for factual consistency, and remained the same or improved with LLM-as-a-Judge. Variability in evaluator scoring and treatment recommendations may reflect the inherent heterogeneity in acceptable JIA treatment pathways and potential limitations in the LLM-DA’s decision-making logic. Five patient themes were identified: the tool complements rheumatologist expertise, prepares patients through reflection and actionable information, builds confidence for self-advocacy, has variable value depending on the patient-physician relationship, and has potential for broader JIA self-management. These exploratory findings provide a proof-of-concept for using AI to support collaborative decision-making, while highlighting the need for future studies to determine whether LLMs can reliably support clinical practice.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Generative AI has not created the governance crisis in higher education credentialing; it has made it harder to ignore. The academic degree is higher education’s principal instrument for governing access to occupations. Its signaling value depends on assessed work reflecting individual competence. AI weakens that link: in blind marking, AI-written exam answers went largely undetected and, on average, outscored students, while detection tools trail each new model. Strengthening surveillance restores procedural control only at the cost of assessment validity. Drawing on credentialism and signaling theory, this paper argues that the response may need to include institutional redesign, not only pedagogical adjustment. It proposes a degree-free model, illustrated by the yeshiva: a centuries-old institution organized around formation, community, and recognized mastery rather than certification. Labor markets already partly follow this logic, as employers substitute direct observation of performance for the degree within three to five years of hire. Three recommendations follow. Outside safety-critical fields, institutions could stop issuing degrees while continuing to teach. Public investment should shift from surveillance-based assessment toward authentic evaluation. Reform should be differentiated by field, retaining mandatory credentialing in licensed and safety-critical professions. The model is offered as a proposition for debate, not a blueprint.

This study aims to analyze the effect of implementing Big Data and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based financial technology on increasing financial inclusion in Indonesia during the period 2019–2024. The background of this study is based on the rapid increase in digital transformation in the financial sector triggered by the adoption of fintech, but there is still a gap in financial access, especially among low-income groups and disadvantaged regions. This study uses a quantitative approach with a panel data model, involving independent variables of Gross Regional Domestic Product (GRDP), education level, average internet access, fintech loan recipient entities, and the number of mobile banking users on the dependent variable of the Financial Inclusion Index. The data was obtained from official publications of the Financial Services Authority (OJK), Bank Indonesia (BI), and the Central Statistics Agency (BPS). The results of the analysis show that Big Data and AI have a positive and significant contribution to expanding financial inclusion through increased credit distribution efficiency, expanded access to digital services, and personalized financial products. However, their influence is still limited by gaps in digital literacy, infrastructure, and trust in data security. The findings of this study are expected to provide strategic input for regulators, fintech industry players, and academics in formulating technology-based inclusive policies to achieve sustainable national financial inclusion targets.

Phishing protection must operate across heterogeneous attack channels, changing adversarial tactics, and stringent deployment constraints. Although recent studies report substantial gains from machine learning, deep learning, transformer-based language models, and ensemble classifiers, predictive accuracy alone does not establish whether a detector is appropriate for a particular cybersecurity setting. This article critically synthesizes fifteen peer-reviewed studies published during 2022–2026, together with authoritative authentication and e-mail security standards, to examine the applicability of conventional and artificial-intelligence-based phishing analysis and prevention techniques. A structured taxonomy distinguishes reputation and rule systems, lexical and structural URL analysis, e-mail semantics, sequence models, transformer architectures, ensembles, continual learning, and explainability mechanisms. This article introduces a context-aware applicability framework that separates minimum operational requirements from multi-criteria comparison of security efficacy, cross-source generalization, false-alarm burden, latency, resource cost, interpretability, dependency, maintainability, and preventive actionability. A reproducible evaluation protocol is specified for public URL and e-mail corpora, with safeguards against duplicate and domain leakage, temporal drift, misleading class prevalence, and incomplete end-to-end latency accounting. The evidence supports conditional rather than universal selection: inexpensive lexical models are attractive at browser and mobile endpoints; contextual text analysis adds value at e-mail gateways; and ensemble, adaptive, and explainable components are most useful when their operational overhead can be justified. The proposed defense-in-depth architecture couples detection to warnings, quarantine, phishing-resistant authentication, reporting, and incident response.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping human agency, knowledge production, decision-making, and social relations, raising ethical questions about personhood, responsibility, and technological governance. Although existing scholarship addresses relational personhood, Ubuntu, decolonial AI, indigenous knowledge, data justice, and responsible innovation, ancestral ontology and cultural memory remain comparatively underexplored in AI ethics. This study examines how African, particularly Igbo, cosmological understandings of personhood, relationality, spirituality, community, and ancestral continuity can inform ethical AI development and governance. It aims to develop an Ancestral-Relational AI Ethics Framework (AR-AIEF) that integrates African philosophical insights into contemporary debates on technological personhood and accountability. Methodologically, the study adopts a qualitative, non-empirical philosophical design combining conceptual analysis, hermeneutical interpretation, and a critical interdisciplinary review of relevant philosophical, theological, cultural, and AI ethics literature. As a conceptual inquiry, it involves no human participants or statistical sampling. The analysis identifies relational personhood, distributed responsibility, ancestral continuity, intergenerational accountability, communal justice, and human flourishing as key principles for an African-informed approach to AI ethics. It does not equate AI systems with ancestors or attribute spirituality to machines; rather, ancestral relationality provides a lens for examining how AI stores, reproduces, simulates, and mediates cultural memory and human identity. The study contributes an African cosmological perspective to global AI ethics and recommends culturally plural governance, indigenous epistemic participation, protection of ancestral knowledge, meaningful human accountability, and intergenerationally responsible innovation. It argues that ethical AI must consider not only technological capabilities but also the communal relationships and human futures those capabilities shape.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This technical pre-print presents the operational architecture and experimental methodology of Apex Horizon, a mission-critical cyber-physical geospatial telemetry platform designed for real-time natural hazard nowcasting, environmental monitoring, and microclimate risk mitigation under degraded communication infrastructure. The system establishes an auditable multi-stream data architecture integrating open earth-observation feeds: geostationary satellite clean infrared radiometry (NOAA GOES-16 ABI and JMA Himawari-9 AHI), shortwave infrared differential fog detection (ΔTfog), synoptic aviation METAR observations, multi-source anemometer arrays, and seismic feeds. To evaluate operational robustness across distinct climatic regimes, the platform employs a dual-theater operational testbed spanning subtropical continental basins and temperate archipelago zones. Furthermore, the architecture integrates a reproducible three-tier data persistence model (relational, geospatial via PostGIS, and high-dimensional vector similarity indexing via pgvector with HNSW) to decouple raw sensor streams, upstream service trust metrics, and edge heuristic baselines. Experimental evaluation demonstrates complete telemetry preservation through an offline-first synchronization engine and resilient localized situational awareness during central backhaul outages.

This research analyzes the application mechanisms, pedagogical significance, and upcoming challenges of personalized and adaptive learning models in computer science classes within the modern digital educational environment. Against the background of the inadequacy of traditional "one-size-fits-all" instructional methods for students with varying learning paces and prior knowledge, the role of adaptive technologies based on artificial intelligence, machine learning, and Learning Analytics is substantiated. The paper explores the positive impact of intelligent code editors, auto-graders, and dynamic adaptive testing on instructional quality, student motivation, and the development of algorithmic thinking. Simultaneously, strategic issues such as the digital divide, data privacy, and the necessity of implementing a blended learning framework are evaluated.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This eight-week randomized study examined how the order of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) feedback shaped revision and near-term independent writing among 132 Chinese English-as-a-foreign-language (EFL) undergraduates. Students received argument-first (AF; n = 67) or language-first (LF; n = 65) feedback; 64 pairs underwent within-class, within-pair randomization, and four unmatched students were randomized within class. Both modules were independently generated from each initial draft (D0) and locked before release. Students completed two revisions (D1 and D2) across three tasks and a new-topic, AI-free transfer task. Adjusted AF–LF differences in D0–D2 change favored AF for overall quality (0.811 points, 95% CI [0.424, 1.198]) and argumentation (1.102 points, 95% CI [0.668, 1.536]), but not language quality (0.020 points, 95% CI [−0.381, 0.420]). Revision depth and implementation showed stage-specific crossovers. Language contrasts did not survive primary Holm adjustment, although complete-pair sensitivity analysis detected a crossover. Argumentation transfer favored AF (1.057 points, 95% CI [0.508, 1.606]); overall transfer was less consistent, with the complete-pair interval including zero (0.685 points, 95% CI [−0.111, 1.481]). Module type was structurally linked to release stage, so stage-specific contrasts describe sequence-by-stage configurations rather than isolated content or order effects. The findings support cautious use of staged feedback when argumentative development is the instructional priority.

The fast incorporation of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education has changed how university students’ access, evaluate, produce, and communicate scientific information. At the same time, English reading motivation remains significant for Pakistani college undergraduate students because English is extensively used in academic, educational, lingua franca and scientific contexts. English language is also enjoying prestigious status in Pakistan. This study examines AI literacy and English reading motivation as predictors of science communication skills among Pakistani students. AI literacy is theorized as students’ ability to understand, use, evaluate, and ethically engage with AI technologies, while English reading motivation refers to students’ interest in reading for educational, academic and other purposes.
